content: TNX-901 is a pharmaceutical agent currently undergoing clinical trials at the National Jewish Medical and Research Center and other research facilities across the United States. This drug is hypothesized to mitigate allergic reactions triggered by trace amounts of peanuts, such as those inadvertently present in food products. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has granted TNX-901 fast-track status, a designation reserved for drugs addressing unmet medical needs. TNX-901 is developed by Tanox, a biotechnology company based in Houston. However, the development of this drug has been entangled in legal disputes. The contention arises from allegations that the drug's underlying anti-asthma science was funded by Genentech and Novartis, leading to a patent infringement lawsuit. These legal challenges have delayed the progress of TNX-901's clinical trials. The drug functions as an anti-IgE antibody. Immunoglobulin E (IgE) is a receptor that plays a pivotal role in initiating allergic reactions and severe asthma exacerbations. Anti-IgE antibodies, such as TNX-901, bind to IgE molecules, thereby preventing them from triggering allergic responses. In clinical trials, individuals with severe peanut allergies who previously exhibited symptoms after consuming the equivalent of half a peanut were able to tolerate up to nine peanuts before experiencing allergic symptoms. While TNX-901 does not cure peanut allergies, it has the potential to prevent severe reactions caused by accidental exposure to peanuts. It is important to note that these trials did not include individuals with life-threatening peanut allergies from trace exposures. A similar drug, Xolair (generic name omalizumab), is already available on the market for the treatment of asthma. However, Xolair is not FDA-approved for use in food allergies. Furthermore, the manufacturer of Xolair has filed a lawsuit against Tanox, claiming patent infringement, which has prevented the release of TNX-901. Although it is possible to obtain a prescription for Xolair for off-label use in food allergies, most health insurance providers do not cover the cost without FDA approval. Consequently, the out-of-pocket expense for patients could amount to approximately $1,000 per month. Recently, Tanox has decided to discontinue the development of TNX-901 in exchange for financial compensation from Genentech and Novartis. The three companies have agreed to collaborate on researching the use of Xolair for peanut allergies instead of pursuing TNX-901. As of July 2004, Xolair has entered Phase II clinical trials to evaluate its efficacy in treating peanut allergies.
